name: Vera Walsh

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making the time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We aren't tied to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, and your name won't be attached to it. To start, can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work at a warehouse that supplies chemist shops: paracetamol, plasters, shampoo, baby formula. I'm on the day shift, permanent since the spring. I pick into grey totes, one tote per shop, and every medicine has a batch number you have to scan, so it's slower than it sounds. Then the totes go on a conveyor to be sealed and loaded.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What wears you out most, and what do you actually like about it?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: The batch scanning wears me out, because if you grab the wrong batch you get pulled up, and I still do it more than I should. I like that it's clean and warm, compared to the frozen food place I tried first. My partner Tom's an apprentice mechanic, so between us we earn about one proper wage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. I'll read it as written. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say makes sense, a lot of new things get oversold. At work we'd probably laugh about the AI scheduling app that still can't get the break rota right. I wouldn't post anything, I don't really post.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me it's mostly fine, but fine isn't great. I'm permanent and I like the place. The worry is just the money, which was a worry before anyone said AI.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep my head down and try to get onto goods-in, where they check deliveries against the paperwork, because it pays a bit more. I'd keep using the AI app for meal plans on a budget, like I already do sometimes. And I'd try to save 30 a month for once.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Steady, a bit stuck. Like treading water in a warm pool.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said one proper wage between you. What does a bad month look like?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My partner Tom's car needing a part is what a bad month looks like. Then the rent's late and we're both ringing our mums. It's happened twice this year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Do you want to stay picking?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not forever. Goods-in is the next step up, then maybe stock control. I'm not ambitious exactly, I'd just like a bit more each month.

say: New things often get **oversold**, so this makes sense.
We'd laugh at work about the **scheduling app** that still can't sort the break rota.
think: I'm **permanent** and like the place, so work feels mostly fine.
The real worry is **money**, which existed before anyone mentioned AI.
do: Apply to move onto **goods-in**, checking deliveries for a bit more pay.
Keep using the **AI app** for budget meal plans.
feel: **Steady but stuck**, like treading water in a warm pool.
S0.quote: My partner Tom's car needing a part is what a bad month looks like. Then the rent's late and we're both ringing our mums.
fieldNote: Her job feels **secure**, but money is fragile: late rent twice this year.
Her ambition is **modest and practical**: goods-in, then stock control.
She uses **AI casually**, for budget meal plans, without strong feelings about it.

steps.text: Apply to move onto goods-in checking deliveries for slightly more pay
Save 30 a month from her day-shift pay

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second one is called Steady Disruption. I'll read it as written. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a change, but we've had changes before. Scanners came in, new conveyors came in, and we're still here. I'd tell people to wait and see before getting worked up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it messes up my plan. Goods-in is checking paperwork against deliveries, and that's exactly the thinking stuff that goes to software first. Picking would carry on a while, but the step up I wanted might disappear.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep picking and watch which jobs the company keeps hiring for. When a couple of people had done the new training and it worked out, I'd sign up too. I'd also ask whether they need people to keep the robots and conveyors running, because that's still hands.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. Like I was climbing a ladder and somebody took the next rung.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said goods-in might not be the step up anymore. What would be?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe the person who handles the robots and the faults. Or the forklift side, because forklifts on a busy dock are hard to automate quickly. I'd ask Tom, he knows machines.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at work would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Brenda on goods-in, who's 58. She's brilliant at spotting a dodgy batch, but she'd have to learn a new system at the end of her career.

say: We've had **changes before**, like scanners and conveyors, and we're still here.
I'd tell people to **wait and see** before getting worked up.
think: **Goods-in** is paperwork checking, exactly the work that goes to software first.
Picking lasts a while, but my **step up** might disappear.
do: Keep picking and **watch which jobs** the company keeps hiring for.
Sign up for **new training** once a couple of colleagues have done it.
Ask about **robot and conveyor** maintenance roles.
feel: **Anxious**, like someone took the next rung off my ladder.
S1.quote: Goods-in is checking paperwork against deliveries, and that's exactly the thinking stuff that goes to software first.
fieldNote: She spots that her **planned promotion** is a thinking job, exposed first.
She'd **follow others** into training rather than lead, true to her steady nature.
Her partner's **mechanic skills** shape her interest in machine roles.

steps.text: Watch which warehouse roles keep getting hired before choosing
Join company training once two colleagues have done it successfully
Ask about conveyor and robot maintenance roles at the chemist warehouse

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third one is called AGI by 2028. I'll read it as written. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say nobody's ready for this, including the government. I'd probably share posts asking what the plan is for normal people, which isn't like me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means I've got about five years of picking and then nothing I'm trained for. Goods-in goes in 2028, picking goes around 2031. Tom's mechanic trade might hold a bit longer, so we'd lean on that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first year I'd do whatever proven course looks safest, probably forklift and maybe a maintenance basics course. I'd use the AI tools more, since everybody would be. Tom and I would put off moving in together properly and stay in the shared house to save rent.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. Properly frightened for the first time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: So the thinking side changes in 2028 and robots for hands-on work come around 2031. What happens in between?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Three years of watching, honestly. The office empties out, the screens start telling us everything, and everyone wonders who goes first. I'd try to make myself useful on the machines before then.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you and Tom cut first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The flat we were going to get together, that's first. Then takeaways, and Tom's football. We'd stay in the shared house with the noisy neighbours another few years.

say: I'd share posts asking what the **plan** is for normal people, which isn't like me.
think: I've got about **five years** of picking, then nothing I'm trained for.
Tom's **mechanic trade** might hold longer, so we'd lean on that.
do: Take the **safest proven course**, like forklift or maintenance basics.
Use the **AI tools** more, since everybody would be.
Postpone **moving in** together and stay in the shared house.
feel: **Alarmed**, properly frightened for the first time.
S2.quote: Goods-in goes in 2028, picking goes around 2031.
fieldNote: She lays out a clear **timeline** of her own job's end using the robot delay.
The couple would **postpone their own flat**, a real family-plan change.
She'd lean on **Tom's trade** as the safer household income.

steps.text: Take a forklift licence and a maintenance basics course
Use AI tools more at work as everyone adopts them
Postpone moving into a flat with Tom and stay in the shared house

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth one is called AGI by 2031. I'll read it as written. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say there's time to sort it if people stop panicking. I'd tell friends to watch what the first movers do and copy what works.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd have till about 2034 for picking. That's long enough to see which jobs survive. I'd hate wasting money on a course that leads nowhere.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stay picking, save 40 a month, and in the second or third year do whichever course my mates found worked. I'd probably try for a maintenance trainee role. I'd use the AI tools as they become normal at work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but able to breathe.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you still delay the flat with Tom?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably not. We'd move in together, just somewhere cheaper. Life doesn't wait for robots.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which course would you trust?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd trust a course where somebody I know got a job out of it. Not an advert.

say: There's **time to sort it** if people stop panicking.
I'd tell friends to watch the **first movers** and copy what works.
think: I'd have until about **2034** for picking, enough to see which jobs survive.
I'd hate **wasting money** on a course that leads nowhere.
do: Keep picking and save **40 a month**.
Take whichever **course** worked for friends in year two or three.
S3.quote: I'd trust a course where somebody I know got a job out of it. Not an advert.
fieldNote: She'd **copy proven paths**, trusting friends over adverts.
Five years lets her **keep life plans**, moving in with Tom somewhere cheaper.
Her job still **ends**, so the worry stays real.

steps.text: Save 40 a month from her picking wage

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last one is called AGI by 2036. I'll read it as written. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say great, that's time to sort ourselves out. Ten years is a career change, easy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not easy, but doable. I'd be nearly 40 when robots can pick. I'd want to be off the floor by then, but I've got time to see what works.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This year, try for goods-in anyway, because it's still there for a few years and pays more. Then around year three, do a maintenance course once others have proven it. Save steadily, even small amounts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. It's still coming, but it's not on top of me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Ten years. Any chance you'd relax and do nothing?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe. Tom would push me though, he's good at that. And I'd see colleagues doing courses, which always gets me moving.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Where would you want to be by then?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: By 2036 I want to be fixing the conveyors instead of feeding them. A flat with Tom. Maybe kids, if we can afford it.

say: Ten years is time to **sort ourselves out**.
A **career change** in a decade sounds easy when you say it out loud.
think: I'd be **nearly 40** when robots can pick.
It's **doable**, not easy, with time to see what works.
do: Try for **goods-in** this year, since it pays more for now.
Take a **maintenance course** around year three, once proven.
feel: **Uneasy**, with the change coming but not on top of me.
S4.quote: By 2036 I want to be fixing the conveyors instead of feeding them.
fieldNote: She says **uneasy**, but her job still goes and her cushion is thin, so it's anxious.
Her plan **stages** carefully: goods-in now, maintenance later.
Colleagues and **Tom's push** are what get her moving.

steps.text: Apply for goods-in this year for the higher pay
Take a conveyor maintenance course around year three
Save small amounts every month without skipping

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028. Not enough time to see what works before I'd have to choose. What would help is a list from someone neutral of which jobs are actually hiring, and courses that are paid while you do them.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask about couples. If my partner Tom's trade holds and mine doesn't, we'd manage. If both go, I don't know.

headlineQuote: If my partner Tom's trade holds and mine doesn't, we'd manage. If both go, I don't know.
portrait: Vera is a **27-year-old picker** at a warehouse for chemist shops, permanent but still slow on batch scanning.
She and Tom, an **apprentice mechanic**, earn roughly one proper wage and were late with rent twice.
She's **pragmatic and steady**, copying what works for others rather than going first.
She realises her planned move to **goods-in** is exposed to AI before her picking job.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, with not enough time to see what works before choosing.
whatWouldHelp: A **neutral list** of which jobs are actually hiring.
**Paid courses** that pay while you train.
